source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 27 (PDF 160-177, printed 157-174); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 27 (Biochemistry), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Biochemistry is the branch of science that deals with:

options.text: chemical substances found in living organisms and their reactions
minerals found in rocks and soil only

blocks.explanation: Biochemistry studies the chemical substances found in living organisms and the reactions they undergo (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Biochemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study of chemical substances found in living organisms

blocks.prompt: 2 The biological compounds contain functional groups that are:

options.text: found only in living cells and never in simple organic compounds
only inorganic ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻
the same types as those found in simple organic compounds

blocks.explanation: Biological compounds are complex molecules with the same functional groups as simple organic compounds: alcohol, amine, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, ester and amide (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: same types of functional groups those found in simple organic compounds

blocks.prompt: 3 Which of the following is NOT one of the essential biomolecules studied in this chapter?
blocks.explanation: The essential biomolecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids; polythene is a synthetic polymer (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: This chapter focuses on the essential biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids

blocks.prompt: 4 Chemically, carbohydrates are:

options.text: esters of fatty acids with glycerol
polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or their derived compounds

blocks.explanation: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or compounds derived from them (27.1).

book_ref.quote: Chemically, they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or their derived compounds.

blocks.prompt: 5 Besides sugars, starch and cellulose, carbohydrates include substances found in:

options.text: bones and teeth as calcium salts
bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons

blocks.explanation: Carbohydrates include sugars, starch, cellulose and substances found in bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons (27.1).

book_ref.quote: substances found in bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons

blocks.prompt: 6 The simplest carbohydrates which cannot be hydrolysed further into simpler compounds are:
blocks.explanation: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates; they cannot be hydrolysed further (27.1).

book_ref.quote: They cannot be hydrolysed further into simpler compounds.

blocks.prompt: 7 In the general formula of monosaccharides, Cₙ(H₂O)y, n ranges from:
blocks.explanation: The general formula of monosaccharides is Cₙ(H₂O)y with n from three to seven (27.1).

book_ref.quote: where n ranges from three to seven

blocks.prompt: 8 A monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms is called a:
blocks.explanation: Triose 3 C, tetrose 4 C, pentose 5 C, hexose 6 C (27.1).

book_ref.quote: a pentose has five carbons, and a hexose contains six carbons

blocks.prompt: 9 Fructose is classified as a:
blocks.explanation: Glucose has an aldehydic group (aldose); fructose has a ketonic group (ketose) (27.1).

book_ref.quote: Glucose is an aldose whereas fructose is a ketose.

blocks.prompt: 10 Which pair consists of monosaccharides only?
blocks.explanation: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides; sucrose is a disaccharide (27.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Examples of monosaccharides are glucose and fructose.

blocks.prompt: 11 Pentoses and hexoses are more stable and more abundant as:
blocks.explanation: Sugars with five or six carbon atoms are more stable as cyclic structures than as open chains (27.1).

book_ref.quote: are more stable and hence more abundant as cyclic structures than as open chain structures

blocks.prompt: 12 The five-membered ring formed by fructose is known as:
blocks.explanation: Fructose forms a five-membered furanose ring; glucose forms a six-membered pyranose ring (27.1).

book_ref.quote: fructose forms a five-membered ring known as furanose

blocks.prompt: 13 The ring of glucose is:
blocks.explanation: Glucose has a six-membered ring known as pyranose (27.1).

book_ref.quote: whereas glucose has a six-membered ring known as pyranose

blocks.prompt: 14 In aqueous solution, glucose molecules exist mostly as:

options.text: rings in the solid but open chains only in solution
rings, in equilibrium with a very small amount of the open-chain form

blocks.explanation: Book correction: in solution most monosaccharide molecules are rings, in equilibrium with a very small amount (well under 1% for glucose) of the open-chain form (27.1).

book_ref.quote: In solution, too, most monosaccharide molecules are rings

blocks.prompt: 15 Pure monosaccharides are solids because of:

options.text: extensive hydrogen bonding between their many –OH groups

blocks.explanation: Many –OH groups cause extensive hydrogen bonding between the molecules, so monosaccharides are solids (27.1).

book_ref.quote: results in the extensive hydrogen bonding between their molecules

blocks.prompt: 16 Monosaccharides are highly soluble in water because they:

options.text: form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules

blocks.explanation: In solution, monosaccharides form extensive hydrogen bonding with water molecules (27.1).

book_ref.quote: they form extensive hydrogen bonding with water molecules, making them highly soluble in water

blocks.prompt: 17 Which sugar is called blood sugar?
blocks.explanation: Glucose is called blood sugar due to its presence in human blood (27.1).

book_ref.quote: Glucose is called blood sugar due to its presence in the human blood

blocks.prompt: 18 The thickness and viscosity of honey are due to:

options.text: strong hydrogen bonding of its glucose and fructose

blocks.explanation: Honey contains glucose and fructose in high concentration; their strong, intensive hydrogen bonding makes it thick (27.1).

book_ref.quote: The thickness and viscosity of honey is due to their strong and intensive hydrogen bonding.

blocks.prompt: 19 The general formula of the common disaccharides is:
blocks.explanation: Disaccharides generally have the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (Disaccharides).

book_ref.quote: generally with the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁

blocks.prompt: 20 The C–O–C bond joining two monosaccharide units is called the:
blocks.explanation: Two monosaccharides are joined via a glycosidic linkage, the C–O–C bond (Disaccharides).

book_ref.quote: The bond C–O–C is known as the glycosidic bond.

blocks.prompt: 21 When two monosaccharides join to form a disaccharide by condensation, the molecule released is:
blocks.explanation: In the condensation reaction a molecule of water is released (Disaccharides).

book_ref.quote: releasing a molecule of water

blocks.prompt: 22 Sucrose (table sugar) is a disaccharide made of:
blocks.explanation: Sucrose, the common table sugar, is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose (Disaccharides).

book_ref.quote: is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose

blocks.prompt: 23 Which of the following is NOT one of the common disaccharides?
blocks.explanation: Sucrose, lactose and maltose are common disaccharides; starch is a polysaccharide (Disaccharides).

book_ref.quote: Among the most common disaccharides are sucrose, lactose and maltose.

blocks.prompt: 24 Taking C = 12, H = 1 and O = 16, the molar mass of a disaccharide C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ is:

book_ref.quote: Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units joined together via glycosidic linkage

blocks.prompt: 25 The general molecular formula of polysaccharides is:
blocks.explanation: Polysaccharides have high molecular mass with general formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: having general molecular formula, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ

blocks.prompt: 26 On hydrolysis, polysaccharides give:
blocks.explanation: Polysaccharides give simple sugars (monosaccharides) on hydrolysis (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: Polysaccharides give simple sugars, i.e., monosaccharides on hydrolysis.

blocks.prompt: 27 The main storage form of energy in plants is:
blocks.explanation: Starch is the main energy store of plants and consists of glucose units (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: Starch is the main storage of energy in plants

blocks.prompt: 28 The two components of starch are:
blocks.explanation: Starch has two components, amylose and amylopectin (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: It has two components, amylose and amylopectin.

blocks.prompt: 29 The structure of amylose consists of:

options.text: long, unbranched chains with many glycosidic linkages
a double helix of two strands

blocks.explanation: Amylose has long unbranched chains; amylopectin is compact and highly branched (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: Amylose has a long, unbranched chains with many glycosidic linkages.

blocks.prompt: 30 The major structural material of plant cell walls is:
blocks.explanation: Cellulose is the major structural material found in plant cell walls (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: Cellulose is the major structural material found in plant cell walls.

blocks.prompt: 31 Cellulose is rigid and insoluble in water because its chains:

options.text: form strong hydrogen bonds with each other

blocks.explanation: The long unbranched cellulose chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: These chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, making cellulose rigid and insoluble in water.

blocks.prompt: 32 In human food, cellulose is important as:

options.text: the main source of instant energy
a source of essential amino acids

blocks.explanation: Cellulose is very important in human food as fibre, which improves gut health (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: It is very important in human food in the form of fibre

blocks.prompt: 33 'Animal starch' is the name given to:
blocks.explanation: Glycogen, a polymer of glucose stored in animals, is called animal starch (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: It is also called the 'animal starch'.

blocks.prompt: 34 In animals, glycogen is stored mainly in the:
blocks.explanation: Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles of animals (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: that is stored in the liver and muscles of animals

blocks.prompt: 35 Compared with amylopectin, glycogen is:

options.text: similar in structure but more highly branched

blocks.explanation: Glycogen's structure is very similar to amylopectin, but it is more highly branched (Polysaccharides).

book_ref.quote: but it is more highly branched, making it different from starch

blocks.prompt: 36 A sample of polysaccharide (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ has molar mass 48 600 g mol⁻¹. Taking C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, the value of n is:
blocks.explanation: One unit C₆H₁₀O₅ = 72 + 10 + 80 = 162 g mol⁻¹; n = 48 600 ÷ 162 = 300. (270 comes from wrongly using 180.)

book_ref.quote: Polysaccharides are large molecules consisting of a large number of monosaccharide units joined together.

blocks.prompt: 37 Which of the following is a polysaccharide?
blocks.explanation: Starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin are common polysaccharides; lactose and maltose are disaccharides, fructose a monosaccharide.

book_ref.quote: Common examples are starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin.

blocks.prompt: 38 On metabolism, 1 g of glucose provides about:
blocks.explanation: Glucose is easily absorbed and metabolised; 1 g provides about 15.6 kJ (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: with 1 g of glucose providing about 15.6 kJ

blocks.prompt: 39 If 1 g of glucose provides about 15.6 kJ, the energy released from 25 g of glucose is about:
blocks.explanation: Energy = 25 g × 15.6 kJ g⁻¹ = 390 kJ.

book_ref.quote: They are easily absorbed and metabolized to release energy

blocks.prompt: 40 The normal range of blood glucose is:
blocks.explanation: Normally blood glucose ranges between 70-110 mg/dL, fluctuating slightly during the day (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Normally, blood glucose levels range between 70-110 mg/dL

blocks.prompt: 41 Blood glucose levels are controlled by the hormones:
blocks.explanation: Insulin and glucagon control blood glucose levels (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: These levels are controlled by the hormones insulin and glucagon.

blocks.prompt: 42 Excess glucose in the body is stored as:
blocks.explanation: Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

blocks.prompt: 43 Hyperglycemia means:
blocks.explanation: Uncontrolled diabetes can cause hyperglycemia (high blood sugar), which may damage nerves and blood vessels (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Uncontrolled diabetes can cause hyperglycemia (high blood sugar)

blocks.prompt: 44 Diabetes occurs when:

options.text: the liver produces too much glycogen
the body absorbs too little fructose
the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body cannot use it effectively

blocks.explanation: Diabetes is a chronic condition when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body cannot effectively use it (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin

blocks.prompt: 45 Insufficient carbohydrate intake can result in:

options.text: fatigue and reduced physical and mental performance

blocks.explanation: Too little carbohydrate can cause fatigue and reduced physical and mental performance (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: insufficient carbohydrate intake can result in fatigue

blocks.prompt: 46 High intake of fructose causes:
blocks.explanation: Fructose provides energy, but its high intake causes obesity, an excessive accumulation of fat (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Its high intake causes obesity

blocks.prompt: 47 When the body has sufficient carbohydrates for its energy needs, it:

options.text: uses them instead of breaking down proteins or fats

blocks.explanation: With sufficient carbohydrates the body uses them for fuel instead of breaking down proteins or fats (27.1.1).

book_ref.quote: it utilizes these instead of breaking down proteins or fats for fuel

blocks.prompt: 48 Complete hydrolysis of proteins gives:
blocks.explanation: Completely hydrolysed proteins yield amino acids (27.2).

book_ref.quote: When proteins are completely hydrolysed, they yield amino acids.

blocks.prompt: 49 About how many different amino acids link together in various sequences to make proteins?
blocks.explanation: About 20 different amino acids create a wide variety of proteins (27.2).

book_ref.quote: About 20 different amino acids link together in various sequences

blocks.prompt: 50 Which of the following is a protein?
blocks.explanation: Skin, hair, haemoglobin (the red pigment of blood) and muscles are all proteins (27.2).

book_ref.quote: haemoglobin in blood (red pigment)

blocks.prompt: 51 A peptide bond is a type of:
blocks.explanation: A peptide bond is an amide bond between two amino acids (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: A peptide bond is an amide bond

blocks.prompt: 52 A peptide bond forms when the –COO⁻ group of one amino acid reacts with which group of the next amino acid?
blocks.explanation: The –COO⁻ group reacts with the protonated amino group –NH₃⁺ (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: reacts with the -NH₃⁺ group of the adjacent amino acid

blocks.prompt: 53 Long chains of amino acids formed by many peptide linkages are called:
blocks.explanation: Long chains of amino acids joined by many peptide linkages are polypeptide chains (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: are called polypeptide chains

blocks.prompt: 54 Proteins are organised into how many structural levels?
blocks.explanation: The four levels are primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Proteins are organized into four structural levels

blocks.prompt: 55 The primary structure of a protein is:

options.text: the specific linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
the coiling of the chain into an α-helix
the folding due to side-chain interactions
the association of two or more folded chains

blocks.explanation: Primary structure is the specific linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: is the specific linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds

blocks.prompt: 56 Sickle cell anemia is caused by:
blocks.explanation: Sickle cell anemia: red blood cells deform into a sickle shape due to abnormal formation of haemoglobin (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This is caused by abnormal formation of haemoglobin.

blocks.prompt: 57 In an α-helix, hydrogen bonds form:

options.text: between the chain and water only

blocks.explanation: In an α-helix, hydrogen bonds form along a single chain, giving a coiled spiral (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: In an α-helix, hydrogen bonds form along a single chain

blocks.prompt: 58 An example of a protein with an α-helix structure is:
blocks.explanation: Keratin has the coiled α-helix; silk fibroin has β-pleated sheets (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: creating a coiled, spiral structure (e.g., keratin)

blocks.prompt: 59 β-pleated sheets form when hydrogen bonds occur between adjacent polypeptide strands. An example is:
blocks.explanation: β-pleated sheets give a folded, sheet-like structure, e.g. silk fibroin (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: giving a folded, sheet-like structure (e.g., silk fibroin)

blocks.prompt: 60 Which of the following is NOT one of the side-chain interactions that form the tertiary structure of a protein?
blocks.explanation: Tertiary structure forms by R-group interactions: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges. Phosphodiester linkages belong to nucleic acids.

book_ref.quote: including hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and disulphide bridges

blocks.prompt: 61 The quaternary structure of a protein arises when:

options.text: a single chain coils into a helix
two or more folded polypeptide chains (subunits) associate
amino acids join by peptide bonds

blocks.explanation: Quaternary structure: two or more folded chains (subunits) associate through hydrogen bonds, ionic bridges, hydrophobic interactions and sometimes disulphide bonds (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: arises when two or more folded polypeptide chains (subunits) associate

blocks.prompt: 62 Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
blocks.explanation: Collagen, keratin and myosin are fibrous proteins; enzymes and hormones are globular (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: collagen (connective tissue), keratin (hair, nails, skin), and myosin (muscle)

blocks.prompt: 63 Fibrous proteins are generally:

options.text: insoluble in water, mechanically strong and stable
soluble in water and easily denatured

blocks.explanation: Fibrous proteins are insoluble, strong and stable, so they serve as structural polymers (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: These proteins are generally insoluble in water, mechanically strong, and stable.

blocks.prompt: 64 A protein whose whole molecule is spherical or ovoid is called a:
blocks.explanation: Spherical or ovoid protein molecules are globular proteins (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: If the shape of the whole protein molecule is spherical or ovoid

blocks.prompt: 65 The hardening of egg white on heating, as hydrogen bonds between chains are disrupted, is called:
blocks.explanation: Heat disrupts hydrogen bonding, the chains open up: this is denaturing (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: This is called denaturing of proteins.

blocks.prompt: 66 Milk protein casein coagulates on adding some lemon juice because:

options.text: lemon juice adds sugar to it
the change in pH denatures it

blocks.explanation: Globular proteins are sensitive to pH; lemon juice changes the pH and casein is denatured (coagulated) (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: the milk protein casein is coagulated when the pH of the solution is changed

blocks.prompt: 67 Enzymes and hormones are mostly:
blocks.explanation: Most worker (functional) proteins such as enzymes, hormones and nutrients are globular (27.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Most worker proteins (functional proteins), such as enzymes, hormones, and nutrients are globular proteins.

blocks.prompt: 68 Insulin, produced by the pancreas, is an example of a:
blocks.explanation: Hormonal proteins regulate physiological activities; insulin regulates movement of glucose from blood into cells (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: An example is insulin, which is produced by pancreas

blocks.prompt: 69 Ferritin is a storage protein that stores:
blocks.explanation: Ferritin is found in some bacteria and in plant and animal tissues, where it stores iron (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: in plant and animal tissues, where it stores iron

blocks.prompt: 70 The most abundant proteins in a vertebrate body are:
blocks.explanation: Structural proteins (keratin, fibrin, collagen) are the most abundant in a vertebrate body (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Structural Proteins are most abundant proteins in a vertebrate body.

blocks.prompt: 71 Actin and myosin, which make up the filaments of muscle, are:
blocks.explanation: Actin and myosin make up the thin and thick filaments of muscle and are contractile proteins (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Contractile Proteins, such as actin and myosin

blocks.prompt: 72 Antibodies, which bind specific antigens on pathogens, are examples of:
blocks.explanation: Defensive proteins help fight infection; antibodies bind antigens with high affinity (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: antibodies recognize and bind to specific antigens

blocks.prompt: 73 Haemoglobin, which carries oxygen as blood travels between the lungs and tissues, is a:
blocks.explanation: Transport or carrier proteins move molecules and ions; haemoglobin carries oxygen (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Transport or Carrier Proteins aid in the movement of molecules and ions across cell membranes.

blocks.prompt: 74 Proteins located within the cell membrane that receive chemical signals are called:
blocks.explanation: Receptor proteins are in the cell membrane and receive chemical signals (27.2.2).

book_ref.quote: they receive chemical signals and responses from and to the cells

blocks.prompt: 75 Enzymes are:

options.text: proteins that act as biological catalysts

blocks.explanation: Enzymes are proteins acting as biological catalysts for reactions in living organisms (27.3).

book_ref.quote: Enzymes are proteins that acts as biological catalysts

blocks.prompt: 76 One molecule of carbonic anhydrase converts about one million CO₂ and H₂O molecules to carbonic acid in:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: the turnover is about 10⁶ per second, not per minute (27.3).

book_ref.quote: Carbonic anhydrase converts about one million molecules in one second

blocks.prompt: 77 If one carbonic anhydrase molecule converts about 10⁶ molecules per second, how many does it convert in one minute?
blocks.explanation: Number = 10⁶ s⁻¹ × 60 s = 6.0 × 10⁷ (3.6 × 10⁹ would be one hour).

book_ref.quote: turnover about 10⁶ per second

blocks.prompt: 78 The special site on an enzyme surface which binds the substrate and converts it into products is the:
blocks.explanation: The active site binds the substrate molecule and converts it into the products (27.3).

book_ref.quote: called the active site, which binds the substrate molecule

blocks.prompt: 79 Enzymes are highly specific because:

options.text: they are destroyed after one reaction
the active site has a unique shape that only a specific substrate fits

blocks.explanation: Specificity is due to the unique shape of the active site, which allows only a specific substrate to fit (27.3).

book_ref.quote: This specificity is due to the active site of the enzyme

blocks.prompt: 80 When a substrate enters the active site, the species formed is:
blocks.explanation: A temporary enzyme–substrate complex forms; then products are released (27.3).

book_ref.quote: a temporary enzyme–substrate complex is formed

blocks.prompt: 81 After the products are released, the enzyme:

options.text: remains unchanged and binds another substrate molecule

blocks.explanation: The enzyme remains unchanged and is free to bind another substrate molecule (27.3).

book_ref.quote: the enzyme remains unchanged and free to bind with another substrate molecule

blocks.prompt: 82 The lock and key model of enzyme action was proposed by:
blocks.explanation: Emil Fischer proposed the lock and key model in 1894 (27.3).

book_ref.quote: lock and key model proposed by Emil Fischer in 1894

blocks.prompt: 83 In the lock and key model, the key represents the:
blocks.explanation: The lock is the enzyme, the key is the substrate and the keyhole is the active site (27.3).

book_ref.quote: the lock is the enzyme and the key is the substrate

blocks.prompt: 84 The temperature that gives maximum enzyme activity is called:
blocks.explanation: The temperature and pH giving maximum enzyme activity are the optimum temperature and pH (27.3.1).

book_ref.quote: are called optimum temperature and pH, respectively

blocks.prompt: 85 Enzymatic reactions in the human body occur best at or around:
blocks.explanation: Enzymatic reactions in the human body occur best at or around 37 °C (27.3.1).

book_ref.quote: occur best at or around 37 °C

blocks.prompt: 86 Increasing enzyme or substrate concentration (within a limit) increases the reaction rate because:

options.text: the enzyme is used up faster

blocks.explanation: With more molecules, more binding sites are available and more enzyme-substrate complex forms (27.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the reaction rate increases due to the formation of more enzyme-substrate complex

blocks.prompt: 87 Besides temperature, pH and concentration, enzyme action may also be affected by:
blocks.explanation: Enzyme action may also be affected by co-enzymes, activators and inhibitors (27.3.1).

book_ref.quote: such as co-enzymes, activators and inhibitors

blocks.text: 27.3.2 Role of Inhibitors in Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

blocks.prompt: 88 Small molecules or ions that cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are called:
blocks.explanation: Inhibitors cause enzymes to lose catalytic activity; all prevent the active site from binding a substrate (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are called inhibitors

blocks.prompt: 89 Reversible inhibitors are called competitive inhibitors because they:

options.text: have the same shape as the substrate and compete for the active site

blocks.explanation: They resemble the substrate in shape, so the substrate and inhibitor compete for the active site (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: as they are the molecules having the same shape as that of the substrate

blocks.prompt: 90 The enzyme that oxidises butanedioate (succinate ion) is:
blocks.explanation: Succinate is oxidised by succinate dehydrogenase (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: is oxidized by the enzyme dehydrogenase succinate

blocks.prompt: 91 Malonate (propanedioate ion) inhibits succinate dehydrogenase because:

options.text: it breaks the enzyme's peptide bonds

blocks.explanation: Malonate (⁻OOC–CH₂–COO⁻) resembles succinate (⁻OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COO⁻), so it competes for the active site (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The propandioate ion (malonate) can inhibit this enzyme

blocks.prompt: 92 A reversible (competitive) inhibitor is held at the active site by:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: a reversible inhibitor is held by non-covalent bonds, not a covalent bond as printed (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: a reversible (competitive) inhibitor is held by non-covalent bonds

blocks.prompt: 93 An enzyme to which an irreversible inhibitor is attached:

options.text: regains activity when more substrate is added

blocks.explanation: With an irreversible inhibitor (poisons, antibiotics, anti-metabolites, some drugs) the enzyme loses activity permanently (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: loses enzymatic activity permanently

blocks.prompt: 94 Which irreversible inhibitor kills bacteria by blocking the enzyme trans-peptidase?
blocks.explanation: Penicillin blocks trans-peptidase, the enzyme for bacterial cell-wall synthesis (book correction: penicillin, not insulin) (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: It is penicillin, not insulin, that kills bacteria

blocks.prompt: 95 The enzyme PLA2 in cobra venom causes hemolysis by:

options.text: destroying the red blood cell wall
breaking down the phospholipids of the red blood cell membrane

blocks.explanation: Book correction: a red blood cell has no cell wall; PLA2 breaks down its membrane phospholipids (27.3.2).

book_ref.quote: PLA2 (phospholipase A2) breaks down the phospholipids of the red blood cell's membrane

blocks.prompt: 96 Unlike polysaccharides and proteins, lipids:

options.text: are not polymers, lacking a repeating monomeric unit

blocks.explanation: Lipids are not polymers; they lack a repeating monomeric unit (27.4).

book_ref.quote: lipids are not polymers, lacking repeating monomeric unit

blocks.prompt: 97 Lipids are:

options.text: hydrophilic and insoluble in organic solvents
soluble in water but not in organic solvents
hydrophobic but soluble in organic solvents

blocks.explanation: Lipids are hydrophobic but soluble in organic solvents (27.4).

book_ref.quote: They are hydrophobic but soluble in organic solvents.

blocks.prompt: 98 On the basis of chemical composition, lipids are broadly classified into:
blocks.explanation: Lipids are broadly classified into simple, complex and derived lipids (27.4).

book_ref.quote: Lipids are broadly classified into simple lipids, complex lipids and derived lipids

blocks.prompt: 99 Simple lipids are:

options.text: esters of fatty acids with different alcohols

blocks.explanation: Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with alcohols, sub-classified as fats, oils and waxes (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: These are esters of fatty acids with different type of alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 100 A triglyceride is an ester formed from:

options.text: three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
one glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate
one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids
a long-chain alcohol and one fatty acid

blocks.explanation: Animal fats and vegetable oils are triglycerides: one glycerol + three fatty acids (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: esters formed from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids

blocks.prompt: 101 Lipids made of saturated fatty acids that are solid at room temperature are called:
blocks.explanation: Saturated fatty acids give fats (solid); oils contain unsaturated fatty acids with double bonds (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Saturated fatty acids make lipids that are solid at room temperature and are called fats.

blocks.prompt: 102 Oils contain:

options.text: unsaturated fatty acids with one or more double bonds

blocks.explanation: Oils contain unsaturated fatty acids with one or more double bonds (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Oil contain unsaturated fatty acids with one or more double bonds.

blocks.prompt: 103 Fats are insoluble in water because:

options.text: their fatty acid chains are hydrophobic

blocks.explanation: The hydrophobic fatty acid chains make fats insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The hydrophobic nature of fatty acid chains makes fats insoluble in water

blocks.prompt: 104 Waxes form protective water-repelling coatings because:

options.text: both their chains are nonpolar and hydrophobic

blocks.explanation: Both chains of a wax are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so waxes prevent water from sticking on surfaces (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Both chains are nonpolar and hydrophobic (water-repelling).

blocks.prompt: 105 Beeswax is given in 27.4.1 as an example of:
blocks.explanation: Waxes are long fatty acid chains esterified to long-chain alcohols; those seen in nature include beeswax (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: those seen in nature include beeswax

blocks.prompt: 106 Waxes are widely used in the manufacture of:
blocks.explanation: Waxes are used in pharmaceutical, cosmetic and other industries for lotions, ointments and polishes (27.4.1).

book_ref.quote: in the manufacture of lotions, ointments and polishes

blocks.prompt: 107 A phospholipid molecule has:

options.text: three fatty acids attached to glycerol
two fatty acids and a phosphate group attached to glycerol
one fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol

blocks.explanation: A phospholipid has only two fatty acids on glycerol; the third –OH is linked to a phosphate group (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: has only two fatty acids attached to glycerol instead of three

blocks.prompt: 108 The head of a phospholipid is hydrophilic because:

options.text: the phosphate group makes it polar

blocks.explanation: The phosphate group makes the molecule polar; the hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The third hydroxyl group of glycerol is linked to a phosphate group, which makes the molecule polar.

blocks.prompt: 109 In a phospholipid bilayer formed in water:

options.text: polar ends face outward and non-polar ends cluster together

blocks.explanation: Phospholipids in water form a bilayer; polar ends face outward and non-polar ends cluster in their own layer (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The polar ends face outward and the non-polar ends clustered together

blocks.prompt: 110 Complexes of lipids and proteins that transport cholesterol and triglycerides in the bloodstream are:
blocks.explanation: Lipoproteins transport hydrophobic lipids like cholesterol and triglycerides in the bloodstream (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Lipoproteins are complexes of lipids and proteins

blocks.prompt: 111 Glycolipids, lipids with sugar groups attached, are mostly found in:
blocks.explanation: Glycolipids carry carbohydrate groups and are mostly found in nervous tissue (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: mostly found in nervous tissue

blocks.prompt: 112 Liposomes are ideal for delivering water-soluble cancer drugs because they have:

options.text: a lipid bilayer surrounding a watery core

blocks.explanation: A liposome's lipid bilayer around a watery core encapsulates water-soluble agents and shields them (27.4.2).

book_ref.quote: a lipid bilayer surrounding a watery core

blocks.prompt: 113 Derived (associated) lipids are:

options.text: the hydrolytic products of simple and compound lipids

blocks.explanation: Derived lipids are hydrolytic products of simple and compound lipids, e.g. fatty acids, glycerol, steroids, lipid-soluble vitamins (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: They are the hydrolytic products of simple and compound lipids

blocks.prompt: 114 The steroid nucleus consists of:

options.text: two cyclohexane and two cyclopentane rings
three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring fused together
one benzene ring and three cyclopentane rings

blocks.explanation: The steroid nucleus has three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring fused together, named A, B, C and D (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: They consist of three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring fused together

blocks.prompt: 115 Steroids that have an –OH functional group are called:
blocks.explanation: Many steroids have an –OH group, which puts them into the alcohol class, sterols (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: which put them into the alcohol class (sterols)

blocks.prompt: 116 Which of the following is NOT a steroid?
blocks.explanation: Cholesterol, bile salts, vitamin D and steroid hormones are steroids; ferritin is an iron-storage protein.

book_ref.quote: including cholesterol, bile salts, vitamin D and steroid hormones

blocks.prompt: 117 Terpenes are built from isoprene units. The correct formula of isoprene is:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene, C₅H₈) is CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂; the printed formula is wrong (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene, C₅H₈)

blocks.prompt: 118 Terpenes that contain 40 carbon atoms are known as:
blocks.explanation: Terpenes with 40 carbon atoms are carotenoids (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Terpenes that contain 40 carbon atoms are known as carotenoids.

blocks.prompt: 119 Each isoprene unit (C₅H₈) has five carbon atoms. How many isoprene units make up the carbon skeleton of a carotenoid (40 C atoms)?
blocks.explanation: Number of units = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

book_ref.quote: Lipids present in plants include a wide variety of hydrocarbons called terpenes

blocks.prompt: 120 Steroids are placed with the lipids because they:

options.text: are esters of three fatty acids
have some lipid-like properties, though not formed from fatty acids

blocks.explanation: Steroids are not formed from fatty acids but have some lipid-like properties (27.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Steroids are not formed from fatty acids but have some lipid like properties.

blocks.text: 27.4.4 Nutritional and Biological Importance of Lipids

blocks.prompt: 121 Compared with carbohydrates, lipids on oxidation provide:
blocks.explanation: Lipids give more energy per gram than carbohydrates because of their higher caloric value (27.4.4).

book_ref.quote: They provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates

blocks.prompt: 122 Lipids act as solvents for the transport and absorption of the vitamins:
blocks.explanation: Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and help their absorption (27.4.4).

book_ref.quote: fat vitamins (A, D, E and K)

blocks.prompt: 123 Fats insulate the body from water, heat and electricity because of their:
blocks.explanation: Fats provide insulation from water, heat and electricity due to their non-polar nature (27.4.4).

book_ref.quote: due to their non-polar nature

blocks.prompt: 124 Hibernating animals store extra fat rather than glycogen because fat:

options.text: is a more concentrated source of energy

blocks.explanation: Fat is a more concentrated energy source than glycogen, so stored fat is used effectively (27.4.4).

book_ref.quote: Fat is a more concentrated source of energy compared to glycogen

blocks.prompt: 125 Nucleic acids are polymers made up of:
blocks.explanation: Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information and are polymers of nucleotides (27.5).

book_ref.quote: They are polymers made up of smaller units called nucleotides.

blocks.prompt: 126 The sugar present in DNA is:
blocks.explanation: The sugar is ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA (27.5).

book_ref.quote: The sugars are ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA

blocks.prompt: 127 In nucleic acids, nucleotides are joined together by:

options.text: phosphodiester linkages through the 5' and 3' carbons of the sugar

blocks.explanation: Nucleotides join by phosphodiester linkages with the 5' and 3' carbon atoms of the sugar (27.5).

book_ref.quote: Nucleotides joined together by a phosphodiester linkage

blocks.prompt: 128 The strength and stability of a polynucleotide chain are due to:
blocks.explanation: Phosphodiester linkages are strong covalent bonds giving strength and stability to the chain (27.5).

book_ref.quote: Phosphodiester linkages are strong covalent bonds

blocks.prompt: 129 A gene is:

options.text: a section of DNA that carries the instructions for a specific protein
a type of RNA in ribosomes
a lipid in the cell membrane

blocks.explanation: Each specific protein is made by a specific gene, a section of DNA (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Each specific protein is made by a specific gene; a section of DNA

blocks.prompt: 130 Humans receive from their parents:
blocks.explanation: Genes are organised into chromosomes; humans receive 23 pairs from their parents (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: in humans, we receive 23 pairs of these from our parents

blocks.prompt: 131 Although nearly every cell carries the full set of genes, a red blood cell:

options.text: switches on the keratin gene only
switches on the haemoglobin gene and keeps the keratin gene off

blocks.explanation: Each cell type switches on only the genes it needs: a red blood cell activates the haemoglobin gene, keratin gene off (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: a red blood cell activates the gene for haemoglobin

blocks.prompt: 132 The double helix model of DNA was given in 1953 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1953 Watson and Crick showed that DNA has two polynucleotide chains coiled into a double helix (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick showed that DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains.

blocks.prompt: 133 In the DNA double helix, each chain forms:
blocks.explanation: Each chain forms a right-handed helical spiral and the two chains coil around each other (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Each chain forms a right-handed helical spiral

blocks.prompt: 134 In DNA, adenine (A) is always paired with:
blocks.explanation: A pairs with T and G pairs with C (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Adenine (A) is always opposite to thymine (T)

blocks.prompt: 135 The number of hydrogen bonds between a G–C pair in DNA is:
blocks.explanation: A–T has two hydrogen bonds; G–C has three (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: three hydrogen bonds between G and C pair

blocks.prompt: 136 How many hydrogen bonds hold the DNA segment G-A-C-T-G-G to its complementary strand?
blocks.explanation: G, C, G, G give 4 G–C pairs × 3 = 12; A, T give 2 A–T pairs × 2 = 4; total = 16.

book_ref.quote: There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T pair

blocks.prompt: 137 If one strand of DNA has the sequence A-G-G-T-C-A, the opposite strand has:
blocks.explanation: A pairs with T, G with C: A-G-G-T-C-A → T-C-C-A-G-T (DNA has no U).

book_ref.quote: and guanine (G) and cytosine (C) are opposite to each other

blocks.prompt: 138 The two polynucleotide chains of DNA are opposite to each other, which means:

options.text: the 3' end of one chain faces the 5' end of the other
both chains run in the same direction
the chains are joined by covalent bonds between bases

blocks.explanation: The chains are not identical but opposite: the 3' end of one faces the 5' end of the other (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: '3' end of one faces the '5' end of the other

blocks.prompt: 139 The process in which DNA is copied during the cell cycle, so that each new cell gets a complete set, is:
blocks.explanation: Replication copies DNA so each new cell receives a complete set of genetic material (27.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Replication is the process during the cell cycle in which DNA is copied

blocks.prompt: 140 Unlike DNA, RNA is usually:

options.text: single stranded, though the chain can fold back on itself

blocks.explanation: RNA is usually single stranded, but the chain can fold back to form a helical loop (27.5.2).

book_ref.quote: RNA is usually single stranded unlike DNA

blocks.prompt: 141 The RNA that carries the genetic blueprint copied from DNA in the nucleus is:
blocks.explanation: mRNA carries the blueprint copied from DNA (27.5.2).

book_ref.quote: it carries the genetic blueprint copied from the DNA in the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 142 The RNA that helps to make up the ribosome is:
blocks.explanation: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) helps to make up the ribosome (27.5.2).

book_ref.quote: it helps to make up the ribosome

blocks.prompt: 143 The RNA that translates the nucleotide sequence of mRNA into a sequence of amino acids is:
blocks.explanation: Transfer RNA (tRNA) translates the mRNA sequence into amino acids (27.5.2).

book_ref.quote: it translates the nucleotide sequence in mRNA

blocks.text: 27.5.3 The Genetic Code and Protein Synthesis

blocks.prompt: 144 Copying the genetic instructions for a protein from a DNA gene into mRNA is called:
blocks.explanation: Copying a DNA gene into mRNA is transcription (27.5.3).

book_ref.quote: the genetic instructions for making a protein are copied from a DNA gene into mRNA

blocks.prompt: 145 Reading the mRNA code at the ribosomes and converting it into a sequence of amino acids is called:
blocks.explanation: At the ribosomes the mRNA code is read and converted into amino acids: translation (27.5.3).

book_ref.quote: forming a protein through the process called translation

blocks.prompt: 146 After it is complete, the mRNA strand:

options.text: stays joined to DNA in the nucleus
detaches from DNA, enters the cytoplasm and attaches to ribosomes

blocks.explanation: The complete mRNA detaches from DNA, enters the cytoplasm and attaches to ribosomes (27.5.3).

book_ref.quote: it detaches from DNA and enters the cytoplasm, where it attaches to ribosomes

blocks.prompt: 147 Minerals are inorganic substances which:

options.text: produce no energy but have important functions
are the main source of energy

blocks.explanation: Minerals produce no energy but perform important functions in life processes (Minerals).

book_ref.quote: Although, they produce no energy

blocks.prompt: 148 Which of the following is a macro (major) mineral?
blocks.explanation: Calcium, phosphorus, sodium and chloride (and, per the book correction, potassium, magnesium and sulfur) are macro-minerals; iron, zinc, iodine are trace.

book_ref.quote: The macro-minerals include calcium, phosphorus, sodium and chloride

blocks.prompt: 149 Macro- and micro-minerals are divided by a daily requirement of about:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: the dividing line is about 100 mg per day; mg/dL is a blood concentration, not an amount needed (Minerals).

book_ref.quote: The dividing line is a requirement of about 100 mg per day

blocks.prompt: 150 Which of the following is a micro (trace) mineral?
blocks.explanation: Iron, copper, cobalt, iodine, zinc, manganese and others are micro-minerals; calcium, phosphorus and sodium are macro (Minerals).

book_ref.quote: the micro-elements include iron, copper, cobalt

blocks.prompt: 151 Iron is needed in the body mainly for:

options.text: formation of bones and teeth only
haemoglobin and myoglobin synthesis, to carry oxygen

blocks.explanation: Iron: haemoglobin in red blood cells and myoglobin in muscle cells; needed to carry oxygen (Table 27.1).

book_ref.quote: myoglobin in muscle cells

blocks.prompt: 152 Which mineral helps in the formation of bones and teeth and in normal blood clotting?
blocks.explanation: Calcium: bones and teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction and relaxation, heart and nerve function (Table 27.1).

book_ref.quote: normal blood clotting, muscle contraction and relaxation

blocks.prompt: 153 The mineral that regulates the release and use of body energy (ATP) is:
blocks.explanation: Phosphorus regulates the release and use of body energy (ATP) and is part of phospholipids (Table 27.1).

book_ref.quote: Regulates the release and use of body energy (ATP).

blocks.prompt: 154 The mineral that is found in the hormone insulin is:
blocks.explanation: Zinc is a component of many enzyme systems and is found in insulin (Table 27.1).

book_ref.quote: Found in the hormone insulin.

blocks.prompt: 155 Sodium, potassium and chloride together help in:

options.text: fluid balance, nerve transmission and muscle function

blocks.explanation: Sodium, potassium and chloride maintain fluid balance, nerve transmission and muscle function (Table 27.1).

book_ref.quote: Maintaining fluid balance, nerve transmission, and muscle function
